newsitem.title: UK: International LPG stable, Asian buyers stay away.
newsitem.headline: International LPG stable, Asian buyers stay away.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) markets were largely stable this week.
Trade was stifled by a large industry conference in the U.S., a continued standoff in East Asia as buyers await lower summer prices, and a lack of demand in Europe.

Demand from the key East Asian markets of Japan, South Korea and China remained subdued as buyers awaitED lower prices in April. These markets traditionally buy stocks and fill their tanks during the summer, when spot prices are lowest, and avoid the spot market where possible as spot prices gear up for the winter.
The main price benchmark is Saudi Aramco's Contract Price (CP), against which nearly all spot deals in this market are traded.
One Japanese trader said on Friday that April's CP for propane is widely expected to be between $200 and $220 a tonne, down by up to $70 a tonne from the March level of $270 a tonne.
As a result, prompt demand was limited.

"At this moment there are no outright purchasers," said a trader. The price was assessed around CP -$5/$0 a tonne C+F Japan, fractionally up on a week ago and indicating a change to the freight market between the Mid East Gulf and East Asia.
In the Gulf itself, propane was assessed at CP -$25/-$20 a tonne, while butane was slightly stronger, at CP -$20/-$15 a tonne.
There were rumours an Abu Dhabi Gas Liquefaction Co (Adgas) tender for propane and butane in the ratio of 3:1 was awarded at CP -$17 a tonne, but this was not confirmed.
The north west European market was quiet throughout the week until Thursday, when some deals were done at slightly higher levels.
A large cargo of 8,500 tonnes of propane was traded at $198 a tonne cif Norway for end-March loading on that day, and on the same day a 3,000 tonne coaster was done at $237 a tonne cif Sweden.
The coaster price was unexpectedly high, and was thought to reflect the urgent nature of the buyer's requirement, but the large cargo price was seen as representative of the spot level.

A Scandinavian trader said there was some evidence of tightening towards the end of the month. The higher price was attributed to the rise in the price of naphtha, a competing petrochemical feedstock, over the period.
Propane coasters on a fob basis were also stronger.
Discussion was heard in the range $210/$215 a tonne fob UK.
A problem at a Scottish refinery was seen as partly responsible for the price rise, with a dealer saying that demand from traditional buyers in France and Portugal had been "very low."

He added that the current spot level was "above where it should be," saying that a price of around $15 a tonne above the BP Agreed Price (BPAP) would be more typical at this time of year. The BPAP for March is $186 a tonne.

But butane coasters were in less demand, with cif buyers heard in the high $170's and low $180's a tonne. On a fob basis, discussion was heard in the high $160's a tonne, with little buying interest seen.
The Mediterranean market for propane perked up at the beginning of the week when a large French petrochemical buyer entered the market and bought up to 20,000 tonnes off large ships from Algeria.
This pushed the price up and brought propane back to a competitive level with naphtha. But while some interest was seen on propane, the Mediterranean butane market was extremely quiet, dealers said.
-Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6412
